paras: Every Wednesday at eight, about thirty people sit down in a small room above a bookshop in Sao Paulo. They are not there for popcorn. The film club has met on the same night for eleven years, and the rule has never changed: you watch the film, you stay for twenty minutes afterwards, and you say one thing about it. Nobody has to be clever. Most people are not. You can join at any time, and nobody asks you why you stopped coming.

This month they are watching thrillers, and the room is fuller than usual. Bianca, who runs the club, says that always happens. People come for the thrillers and they stay for the rest of the year. Right now she is turning people away at the door, and in March she is counting empty chairs.

Tonight the film has subtitles, because half the audience is learning English and asked for them. Two women in the second row are arguing quietly about the plot before the film even starts. They are not agreeing, and they are enjoying that more than they will enjoy the film.

Somebody always asks whether the club is going to show series. Bianca says no. A series has twenty episodes and a life of its own, and the club has two hours. She also does not recommend films to new members, because a recommendation ruins the first twenty minutes. Instead she asks them what they watched last, and she listens. She is not teaching anybody about cinema. She is just keeping a room open on a Wednesday.
reading.source: A portrait written for this lesson, from film clubs that work like this one.

choices: To explain how to start your own film club in a bookshop.
To show one small club, the rule it never breaks, and what its month looks like right now.
To argue that thrillers are better than other kinds of film.

items.situation: Say what the club does every Wednesday, in one sentence.
tips: They watch a film and they stay for twenty minutes afterwards.
This is a habit, so the verb stands alone: they watch, not they are watching.

items.situation: Now say what is different about this month.
tips: This month they are watching thrillers, and the room is fuller than usual.
am / is / are + -ing, because it is only this month.

items.situation: Make one of those sentences negative.
tips: The two women are not agreeing about the plot.
The not goes between are and the -ing: are not agreeing.

items.situation: Ask me two questions about right now: one with what, and one with are.
tips: What are you watching at the moment?

items.situation: Say one thing you always do in your free time, and one thing you are doing these weeks.
tips: I usually watch films on the weekend, but at the moment I am watching a series.
Both halves in the same sentence: that is the whole lesson.

items.situation: Somebody asks if you like the series you are watching. Careful with this one.
tips: I like it. Not I am liking it.
Liking is not an action you can watch somebody doing, so it stays simple.

listenings.text: I am not a film person. I want to say that first, because I am about to talk about a film for four minutes and my wife is in the next room laughing at me. Normally I watch football and nothing else. I do not read the reviews, I do not know the directors, and I usually fall asleep before the end of anything. But at the moment I am watching a series about a small town where somebody disappears, and I am watching it alone, at night, which was a mistake. I am on episode six. My daughter recommended it. She is nineteen and she recommends everything, so I ignored her for two months, and now I am sending her messages at one in the morning asking what happens next. She is not answering. She is enjoying this.

I stopped recommending things to people about five years ago, and my life improved immediately. Here is why. When you recommend a film, you are not giving somebody a film. You are giving them your opinion in advance, and they spend the first twenty minutes checking whether they agree with you, instead of watching. And if they do not like it, one of you has to apologise, which is ridiculous, because nothing happened. So now I do the opposite. I ask what they watched last, I ask what they thought, and I say nothing at all about whether it is good. It is slower. It is also the only way I have ever found to have a real conversation about a film. And one more thing, since everybody asks me about subtitles. Put them on, in the same language as the film. You are not cheating. You are reading and listening at the same time, which is what your brain wants to do anyway.
